To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
firms that create innovations and adopt them early tend to be more innovative in the future, and that the adoption of innovations is influenced by the choice of reference group.
firms vary greatly in their choice of reference groups, and that the selection of an innovating reference group increases the likelihood that a firm will create and adopt innovations early.

innovators are more likely than imitators to adopt innovations early and to create innovations themselves, and that innovators are less likely than imitaters to adopt innovations after they become widely accepted.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role that the reference group plays in organizational decision-making and its implications for the diffusion of innovations.
the question of how firms select their reference group, and how this selection affects their innovation behavior.
the adoption of innovations in the population of firms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the innovating firms are the firms which are more innovative, and that this is the case because they have a reference group of innovating firms.

innovating and imitative firms differ in their choice of reference groups, and that these choices are an important source of firm heterogeneities in the rate of adoption of new organizational practices.

innovating firms are more likely to adopt new organizational routines than imitating firms, because innovating firms are likely to be more exposed to other innovative firms, and thus more likely to be influenced by other firms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
firms are not just imitators but also innovators and the two groups differ in their adoption patterns.
the adoption of organizational routines is not only driven by a firm’s own resources but is also influenced by the choice of a reference group.
the selection of an appropriate reference group is an important factor for the success of an innovative firm.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the adoption of organizational innovations can be understood as a two-step process: first, the selection of a group of innovating firms with which a focal firm compares itself, and, second, a comparison of the focal firm's own performance to that of the reference group.

the adoption of innovations by firms is a process that is not only driven by the characteristics of the innovation itself, but also by the characteristics of firms and the reference groups to which they belong.
a key determinant of firm heterogeneity in innovation is the selection of a distinctive group of reference firms.
